metadata.name: dc.description
metadata.content: Enhancing laser-to-ion energy conversion and increasing the maximum ion energy remain central challenges for laser-driven ion sources. We present a two-dimensional Particle-In-Cell investigation of Target Normal Sheath Acceleration using an annular sector target and a flat target under otherwise identical irradiation conditions. An interaction-matched analysis shows that the partially enclosing geometry produces substantially stronger electromagnetic energy coupling and a hotter energetic-electron population. The terminal closed-control-surface electromagnetic coupling/retention proxy increases from 0.156 for the flat target to 0.616 for the annular sector target, while the median electron slope temperature over $$0\le \tau \le 50$$ fs increases from 0.94 to 4.46 MeV. At $$\tau \simeq 400$$ fs after laser–target contact, the proton cutoff obtained using a common relative spectral threshold increases from 9.29 to 16.82 MeV. The hotter energetic-electron population, together with the species-resolved energy-transfer and particle-resolved work histories, is consistent with stronger electron heating and the resulting longitudinal sheath work being the primary energetic pathway for the ion-energy increase. Surface-resolved and initial-side trajectory diagnostics additionally show that the curved geometry produces a distinct cavity-directed inner-origin population, while the higher energetic tail is carried by outer-origin ions; the data therefore do not isolate an independent cutoff-energy gain caused solely by geometric ion convergence. These results identify enhanced laser–electron energy coupling, together with geometry-controlled particle transport, as the physically supported basis of the improved acceleration.
